title: ACID, Transactions & Indexes
tagline: The four guarantees that keep your data sane, and the tree structures that make queries fast.

sections.content:
Imagine a bank transfer: $100 leaves account A and arrives in account B. Two separate write operations, separated in time by microseconds. What happens if the server crashes after the debit but before the credit? Without special guarantees, the money simply vanishes — debited from one account, never credited to another. Databases solve this with **transactions** and a contract called **ACID**.

**ACID** stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. These four properties, codified in the late 1970s by Jim Gray and Andreas Reuter, describe what a database must guarantee for every unit of work it processes. They are not optional niceties — they are the minimum bar for software that handles real money, healthcare records, or any data that cannot afford to be wrong.

But correctness alone is not enough. A fully ACID database that takes three seconds to answer `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42` on a million-row table is nearly useless in production. Speed comes from **indexes** — auxiliary data structures that let the database jump directly to matching rows instead of scanning every page on disk. The most common index type, the **B-tree**, is a masterpiece of practical computer science: self-balancing, disk-friendly, and capable of supporting both exact lookups and range queries in O(log n) time.

This chapter builds a deep understanding of both pillars. We will trace a transaction through all four ACID properties, understand what the database actually does on disk to provide these guarantees, explore isolation anomalies and how different isolation levels prevent them, then switch to indexes — how B-trees are structured, when the query planner chooses them, and how to read `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` output to diagnose slow queries. Schema design and normalization get their own chapter; here we stay focused on transactions and indexes.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Application"] --> B["BEGIN TRANSACTION"]
  B --> C["Write 1: Debit $100"]
  C --> D["Write 2: Credit $100"]
  D --> E{"All OK?"}
  E -->|"YES"| F["COMMIT"]
  E -->|"ERROR or crash"| G["ROLLBACK"]
  F --> H["WAL flushed to disk"]
  G --> I["All writes undone"]
  H --> J["Consistent durable state"]
  I --> J
sections.caption: A transaction is an all-or-nothing unit. COMMIT flushes the write-ahead log (WAL) for durability; ROLLBACK erases every partial write.

sections.title: The Restaurant Bill — and the Hotel Safe
sections.content:
Picture splitting a restaurant bill with a friend. The waiter charges your card and marks the table paid. If the terminal crashes mid-swipe, the transaction rolls back — your card shows no charge and the table is still open. Nothing is lost or duplicated. That is **Atomicity**: the charge and the table-mark happen together or not at all.

Now imagine the waiter also records every transaction in a tamper-proof ledger before touching anything else. Even if the restaurant burns down after you sign the receipt, the ledger (stored off-site) proves you paid. That is **Durability** — the write-ahead log is the database's off-site ledger.

**Isolation** is the privacy screen between your table and the next. Your party's unfinished order does not appear on their bill, and their drinks do not show up on yours, even though the kitchen handles both simultaneously.

**Consistency** is the restaurant's rule book: every meal must have a seat, every charge must map to an order. No transaction is allowed to leave the database in a state that violates those rules.

sections.title: Atomicity — All or Nothing
sections.content:
**Atomicity** is the simplest ACID property to understand but surprisingly hard to implement correctly. It guarantees that all the SQL statements in a transaction execute as a single indivisible unit. Either every statement succeeds and the transaction commits, or an error occurs and the database rolls every statement back, leaving the data exactly as it was before `BEGIN`.

How atomicity is implemented differs by engine. **MySQL/InnoDB** and **Oracle** write the *old* version of each modified row to an **undo log** (rollback segment) before changing it. On `ROLLBACK` — or during crash recovery — they apply those undo records in reverse order. Rollback cost is therefore proportional to the work done: a transaction that updated millions of rows can take minutes to undo.

**PostgreSQL** has no undo log. Every update writes a *new* row version (see MVCC below), and aborting simply marks the transaction ID as aborted in the commit log (`pg_xact`). Readers then ignore that transaction's row versions, so `ROLLBACK` is near-instant; the dead versions are cleaned up later by `VACUUM`. Either way, keep transactions short: long transactions hold locks, prevent VACUUM from reclaiming space, and — in undo-based engines — are expensive to roll back.

A subtle point: **DDL statements** (`CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, even `DROP TABLE`) are fully transactional in PostgreSQL — you can run a whole migration inside `BEGIN … COMMIT` and roll it back (a few commands, such as `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, refuse to run inside a transaction block). MySQL is different: DDL triggers an **implicit commit** of any open transaction, so a multi-step migration cannot be rolled back as a unit; MySQL 8.0's "atomic DDL" only makes each *single* DDL statement all-or-nothing. Oracle also commits implicitly around DDL.

sections.title: Consistency — Rules That Cannot Be Broken
sections.content:
**Consistency** is the one ACID property that the *application* shares responsibility for with the database. The database enforces the consistency rules you define — primary keys, foreign key constraints, `NOT NULL`, `CHECK` constraints, `UNIQUE` constraints — and guarantees that no transaction can commit if it would violate any of them. But it is up to the developer to define those rules correctly.

For example: if you define a foreign key from `orders.user_id` to `users.id`, the database will reject any attempt to insert an order referencing a non-existent user, or to delete a user who still has orders (depending on your `ON DELETE` clause). Consistency means the database always remains in a **valid state** with respect to these invariants.

Notice that Consistency overlaps with Atomicity and Isolation — it is actually *derived* from them. If every transaction preserves the invariants when run alone, atomicity and isolation guarantee they also hold when transactions run concurrently and crash halfway. This is why some database theorists consider Consistency slightly redundant in the acronym, but it remains important as a reminder that the application must declare its invariants to the database.

Single-row rules such as "balance must never go negative" belong in a `CHECK (balance >= 0)` constraint. **Multi-row invariants** — "at least one doctor must be on call", "ledger entries for a transfer must sum to zero" — cannot be expressed as a `CHECK`. They need application logic inside the transaction plus either `SERIALIZABLE` isolation or explicit locks; at weaker isolation levels two concurrent transactions can each pass the check and jointly break the rule (**write skew**).

sections.title: Isolation — Concurrent Transactions and Their Anomalies
sections.content:
**Isolation** is the most complex ACID property. In production, dozens or thousands of transactions execute concurrently. Isolation controls what each transaction is allowed to *see* of the changes made by others, and which interleavings the database will allow.

The SQL standard defines its levels in terms of three classic anomalies:

**Dirty read**: Transaction A reads a row that Transaction B has modified but not yet committed. If B then rolls back, A has read data that never officially existed.

**Non-repeatable read**: Transaction A reads a row, Transaction B updates and commits that row, then A reads the same row again and gets a different value.

**Phantom read**: Transaction A runs a range query (e.g., `SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE total > 100`) and gets 50. Transaction B inserts a new order with total 150 and commits. A runs the same query again and gets 51 — a "phantom" row appeared.

Two more anomalies matter just as much in practice: the **lost update** (two read-modify-write cycles on the same row, one silently overwriting the other) and **write skew** (two transactions read the same data, each updates a *different* row based on what it read, and together they break an invariant).

The four standard **isolation levels**:

- **Read Uncommitted** — may allow dirty reads. PostgreSQL silently treats it as Read Committed.
- **Read Committed** — the default in **PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server**. Each *statement* sees only data committed before that statement started. Prevents dirty reads; allows non-repeatable reads, phantoms, and lost updates.
- **Repeatable Read** — the default in **MySQL/InnoDB**. Each *transaction* reads from a snapshot taken at its first query. In PostgreSQL this level is **snapshot isolation**: it also prevents phantoms (stronger than the standard requires) and aborts a transaction that tries to update a row someone else changed concurrently — but it still allows **write skew**. InnoDB's plain `SELECT`s read a snapshot too, but its `UPDATE`s and locking reads act on the latest committed rows (using next-key locks), so lost updates are still possible there.
- **Serializable** — the result must equal *some* one-at-a-time ordering of the transactions. Prevents every anomaly above, including write skew. PostgreSQL implements it with **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**: it tracks read/write dependencies and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE `40001`, which the application must retry. MySQL implements it with locking (plain reads take shared locks).

Most PostgreSQL applications run at Read Committed and handle read-modify-write paths explicitly — with an atomic `UPDATE … SET balance = balance - 100`, with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, or by switching that one transaction to `SERIALIZABLE`. The Transaction Isolation Levels chapter goes deeper.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Read Uncommitted"] --> B["Read Committed"]
  B --> C["Repeatable Read"]
  C --> D["Serializable"]
  A -.-> E["Allows: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms"]
  B -.-> F["Allows: non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates"]
  C -.-> G["Allows: phantoms per SQL std, write skew in PostgreSQL"]
  D -.-> H["Allows none, but may abort: retry"]
sections.caption: Each level removes anomalies at the cost of concurrency. Defaults: Read Committed in PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server; Repeatable Read in MySQL InnoDB.

sections.title: Durability — Surviving Crashes with the Write-Ahead Log
sections.content:
**Durability** guarantees that once a transaction commits, the changes survive any subsequent crash — power failure, OS panic, hardware fault. The database achieves this through the **write-ahead log (WAL)**, also called the redo log in some systems.

The WAL works like this: before the database modifies any actual data page in memory (the buffer pool), it first writes a description of the change to a sequential log file on disk. The log is written sequentially, which is far faster than random writes to data pages. Only after the WAL record is safely on disk does `COMMIT` return to the application.

After a crash, recovery replays (redoes) the WAL from the last **checkpoint**, bringing every data page up to date. What happens to transactions that never committed depends on the engine: InnoDB (following the ARIES design) redoes everything and then uses its undo logs to roll back the uncommitted transactions; PostgreSQL leaves their row versions in place but marked as belonging to an aborted transaction, so no reader ever sees them.

This two-phase approach — **WAL then data pages** — gives you the best of both worlds: sequential log writes for performance, and guaranteed recoverability. PostgreSQL calls this **WAL**; MySQL/InnoDB calls it the **redo log**; Oracle calls it the **redo log** as well.

A critical subtlety: `fsync`. A plain `write()` only lands in the OS page cache; the database must call `fsync()`/`fdatasync()` (or open the log with `O_DSYNC`) to force the commit record onto stable storage before acknowledging `COMMIT`. Busy databases batch many concurrent commits into one flush (**group commit**) to amortise that cost. The storage must also be honest: a disk with a volatile write cache that acknowledges a flush early can lose "durable" commits on power loss.

Setting PostgreSQL's `fsync = off` is not a mild trade-off: after an OS crash or power loss the database can be left **corrupted**, not merely missing recent transactions — use it only for throwaway test data. If you want to trade a little durability for speed safely, use `synchronous_commit = off`: the database stays consistent, and a crash loses at most the last few hundred milliseconds of acknowledged commits (up to 3 × `wal_writer_delay`, default 200 ms).

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant App
  participant DB
  participant WAL
  participant DataPages
  App->>DB: BEGIN + write statements
  DB->>WAL: Write change records
  WAL-->>DB: fsync confirmed
  DB->>App: COMMIT OK
  Note over DB,DataPages: Data pages updated lazily
  Note over WAL: On crash: replay WAL to restore
sections.caption: WAL is written and fsynced before COMMIT returns. Data pages are updated asynchronously for performance.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The DO block enforces the non-negative-balance rule by hand; a `CHECK (balance >= 0)` constraint would do the same automatically and can never be forgotten. In PostgreSQL an error does not end the transaction by itself — it puts it in an aborted state, and `COMMIT` then rolls back. `FOR UPDATE` takes a row-level lock so concurrent read-modify-write transactions on the same row run one after another, preventing **lost updates**. Plain `SELECT`s are not blocked by it, thanks to MVCC.

sections.title: MVCC — How Modern Databases Achieve High Concurrency
sections.content:
Locking every row that a transaction reads would serialize all concurrent work and destroy throughput. Modern databases instead use **Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)**. The key idea: instead of locking, the database keeps *multiple versions* of each row, stamped with transaction IDs. Readers see the version that was current when their transaction (or statement, depending on isolation level) started. Writers create a new version rather than overwriting the old one.

In PostgreSQL, every row has hidden system columns: `xmin` (the transaction ID that created this version) and `xmax` (the transaction ID that deleted or superseded it). When you read a row, PostgreSQL checks your transaction's snapshot — the set of transaction IDs that were committed when your snapshot was taken — and returns the row version whose `xmin` is in the snapshot and `xmax` is not.

The consequence is that **readers never block writers and writers never block readers**. Two transactions can both be reading and writing the same table simultaneously without either waiting for the other (unless they write the *same* row, which requires a brief lock).

The cost of MVCC is **dead tuples** (old row versions that no longer match any live snapshot). PostgreSQL's `VACUUM` process periodically reclaims these. A table that receives many updates without regular VACUUM will grow large with dead tuples, causing table bloat and degraded scan performance — a real production concern.

MySQL/InnoDB implements MVCC differently, using a separate **undo tablespace** to reconstruct old row versions rather than storing them inline with live data. The mechanics differ, but the external behavior is similar: high read concurrency with minimal blocking.

sections.title: Indexes — Why Full Table Scans Kill Performance
sections.content:
Consider a `users` table with 5 million rows. Each row is about 200 bytes. That is 1 GB of data stored across tens of thousands of 8 KB disk pages. When you run `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'alice@example.com'`, without an index the database must read *every single page* — a **sequential scan**. On a typical disk, reading 1 GB takes hundreds of milliseconds. On a server under load, with many concurrent queries competing for I/O, that becomes seconds.

An **index** is a separate data structure that maps column values to the physical location of matching rows (heap tuples). Instead of scanning all 5 million rows, the database descends a tree in O(log n) steps — roughly 23 comparisons for 5 million rows — and jumps directly to the matching pages. The difference between a sequential scan and an index scan on a large table is often three to four orders of magnitude in wall clock time.

Every index trades **write overhead for read speed**. When you insert or update a row, every index on that table must also be updated. This is why a table with 20 indexes can be significantly slower to write to than a table with 3 — each write triggers 20 separate index updates. The art of indexing is choosing which columns deserve an index based on the actual query patterns and the write-to-read ratio of the workload.

sections.title: B-Trees — The Index Structure Behind 99% of Database Indexes
sections.content:
The **B-tree** (Balanced tree) was invented by Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight at Boeing in 1970, in a paper titled 'Organization and Maintenance of Large Ordered Indexes' (published in Acta Informatica in 1972). It was designed specifically to work efficiently with *disk storage* — where reading a single page from disk is orders of magnitude slower than reading the next memory word, so minimizing the number of disk reads matters enormously.

A B-tree has three kinds of nodes:

**Root node**: the top of the tree. Every search starts here. In a large index, the root is typically cached permanently in memory.

**Internal nodes**: each holds an array of keys and pointers to child nodes. The keys partition the search space: if you are looking for key K, you follow the pointer between the key just less than K and the key just greater than K.

**Leaf nodes**: the bottom level. Each leaf holds actual index entries — the indexed column value plus a pointer (physical location, called a `ctid` in PostgreSQL or a `rowid` in Oracle) to the actual heap row. In a **B+ tree** (the variant most databases use), all data lives in leaf nodes, and leaf nodes are linked to their siblings for efficient range scans. In MySQL/InnoDB the table itself *is* a B+ tree clustered on the primary key: its leaves hold the full rows, and secondary-index leaves store the primary key value instead of a physical pointer — so a secondary-index lookup is two tree descents.

The `B` in B-tree is sometimes said to stand for Bayer, sometimes Boeing, sometimes Balanced. The defining property is that **all leaf nodes are at the same depth**, and every node is kept between half-full and completely full. Insertions and deletions are followed by rebalancing (splits and merges) to maintain this invariant. This guarantees O(log n) height regardless of insertion order.

A critical disk-friendly property: each node corresponds to one disk page (typically 8 KB in PostgreSQL). A single node can hold hundreds of keys. A B-tree over 1 billion rows typically has a height of only 4–5 — meaning a lookup touches at most 5 disk pages, regardless of table size. Compare that to a binary search tree over the same data, which would have height ~30 and require 30 random disk reads.

sections.caption: B+ tree: a node with k keys has k+1 children (keys ≥ a separator go right). Internal nodes only route searches; all entries live in leaves, which sit at the same depth and are linked left-to-right for range scans (links not drawn).

sections.title: Range Scans, Composite Indexes, and Index-Only Scans
sections.content:
B-trees support not just exact lookups (`WHERE id = 42`) but also **range queries** (`WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-06-30'`). Because leaf nodes are sorted and linked, the database descends to the first matching leaf, then walks the linked list rightward until it exits the range. This is why B-trees vastly outperform hash indexes (which support only equality lookups) for range queries.

**Composite indexes** (multi-column indexes) are powerful but require understanding the **leftmost prefix rule**. An index on `(last_name, first_name)` can serve queries on `last_name` alone or on `(last_name, first_name)` together, but *cannot* use a normal descent for `first_name` alone. The index is sorted first by `last_name`, then by `first_name` within each `last_name`, so matching `first_name` values are scattered across every group. At best the planner scans the whole index (worthwhile only when the index is much smaller than the table or covers the query); PostgreSQL 18 added **B-tree skip scan**, which helps only when the leading column has few distinct values. If you regularly filter on `first_name` alone, give it its own index.

Column order in a composite index matters: put columns compared with **equality** first and the column used for a **range** or `ORDER BY` last — once the descent hits a range condition, later columns can no longer narrow it. Among the equality columns, choose the order that gives your *other* queries a usable leftmost prefix; "most selective column first" is only a weak tie-breaker, not the main rule. An index on `(status, created_at)` works well for `WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at > '2024-01-01'` — the equality predicate on `status` narrows to a small subset, then `created_at` is scanned as a range within that subset.

**Index-only scans** are a performance superpower. If all the columns needed by a query are present in the index itself (either as indexed columns or as `INCLUDE`d columns in PostgreSQL 11+), the database never needs to touch the heap at all. `SELECT email FROM users WHERE email = 'alice@example.com'` with an index on `email` requires only the index — the heap row is never fetched. This eliminates the most expensive part of an index scan: the random heap access.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  Q["Query: WHERE status='pending' AND created_at > 2024"] --> I["Composite Index\n(status, created_at)"]
  I --> L1["Descend to status='pending' section"]
  L1 --> L2["Walk leaves where created_at > 2024"]
  L2 --> H["Fetch heap rows by rowid"]
  H --> R["Return result set"]
sections.caption: Composite index lookup: equality predicate narrows to a subtree, then range scan walks sorted leaves within that subtree.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
-- 1. Create a simple B-tree index (the default type)
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email);

-- 2. Composite index — order matters: equality columns first, range last
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_created
  ON orders (status, created_at DESC);

-- 3. Index with INCLUDE for index-only scans (PostgreSQL 11+)
--    The query below can be satisfied entirely from the index
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_include_name
  ON users (email) INCLUDE (first_name, last_name);

SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users WHERE email = 'alice@example.com';
-- -> Index Only Scan (never touches heap)

-- 4. Partial index — only index the rows you actually query
--    This index is far smaller and faster than indexing all orders
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending
  ON orders (created_at)
  WHERE status = 'pending';

-- 5. EXPLAIN ANALYZE — read the actual execution plan
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT)
  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at > '2024-01-01';
-- Look for:
--   "Index Scan using idx_orders_status_created" -> good
--   "Seq Scan" on large table                    -> needs index
--   actual rows vs. rows estimate divergence     -> stale stats, run ANALYZE
--   Buffers: shared hit=X read=Y                 -> Y > 0 means disk I/O

-- 6. Refresh table statistics (let planner make better decisions)
ANALYZE orders;
sections.explanation: The `INCLUDE` clause stores extra columns in leaf nodes without affecting sort order — they are invisible to the search but available for index-only scans. Partial indexes are a powerful tool: a partial index on `status = 'pending'` is tiny (only pending orders) and blazing fast for the common case of querying open work. `EXPLAIN (BUFFERS)` reveals whether the query hit disk or served from cache — a critical production tuning signal.

sections.title: Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE — Diagnosing Slow Queries
sections.content:
PostgreSQL's `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` is the primary tool for understanding why a query is slow. It executes the query, captures actual row counts and timings at each plan node, and returns the full execution plan. Learning to read it fluently is one of the highest-leverage database skills.

Key terms in the output:

**Seq Scan**: The planner is reading every row in the table. On a small table (<10,000 rows) this is often faster than an index scan because the overhead of the index is not worth it. On a large table with a selective WHERE clause, it almost always means a missing index.

**Index Scan**: The planner uses an index to find rows, then fetches each matching heap row by its physical location. Each heap fetch is a random I/O, which is expensive if many rows match (say, >5-10% of the table). For large result sets, the planner may prefer a sequential scan.

**Index Only Scan**: All needed columns are in the index; no heap access needed. The fastest read path.

**Bitmap Heap Scan**: Used when many rows match the index condition. The database first collects all matching heap locations from the index into a bitmap, sorts them by physical location, then scans the heap in order (converting random I/Os to sequential I/Os). More efficient than a plain Index Scan when many rows match.

**Hash Join / Nested Loop / Merge Join**: Join strategies. Nested Loop is fast when the inner table is small or indexed. Hash Join materializes one side into a hash table — good for large equi-joins. Merge Join works when both sides are sorted on the join key.

**`rows=X` vs `actual rows=Y`**: A large divergence means the planner's statistics are stale. Run `ANALYZE table_name` to update them. Stale statistics are a leading cause of bad query plans.

The number to minimize is **cost** (in arbitrary units) and especially **actual time** in milliseconds. Filter nodes that discard many rows after fetching them suggest the wrong index or a missing composite index covering the filter column.

sections.title: A Note on Schema Design
sections.content: Indexes cannot rescue a badly shaped schema. **Normalization** (1NF/2NF/3NF) removes redundant copies of the same fact so that an update touches one row instead of many; deliberate **denormalization** copies data back onto hot read paths to avoid joins, at the cost of keeping the copies in sync on every write. Both decisions change which indexes you need — the Normalization & Data Modeling chapter covers them in depth. Before denormalizing for speed, check with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`: a join on properly indexed foreign keys is usually fast enough.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
-- Write skew: "at least one doctor must stay on call for shift 7"
-- Two doctors run this at the same time, each for their own id.
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
  SELECT count(*) FROM doctors
  WHERE on_call AND shift_id = 7;          -- both see 2
  -- application: proceed only if count >= 2
  UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false
  WHERE id = 1 AND shift_id = 7;           -- the other one updates id = 2
COMMIT;
-- Under SERIALIZABLE one of them fails (at UPDATE or COMMIT) with
--   ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies
--          among transactions   (SQLSTATE 40001)
-- The application must catch 40001 and re-run the WHOLE transaction.
-- Under READ COMMITTED or REPEATABLE READ both commit -> nobody on call.

-- Alternative at READ COMMITTED: lock the rows the decision depends on
BEGIN;
  SELECT id FROM doctors
  WHERE on_call AND shift_id = 7
  FOR UPDATE;                              -- second caller waits here
  -- application: proceed only if 2+ rows came back
  UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false
  WHERE id = 1 AND shift_id = 7;
COMMIT;
sections.explanation: Each transaction reads the same rows but writes a *different* row, so no write-write conflict ever occurs — that is why snapshot isolation (PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ) lets both commit. SERIALIZABLE (SSI) notices the dangerous read/write dependency cycle and aborts one transaction; retrying it then sees only one doctor on call and stops. The `FOR UPDATE` version forces the two callers to queue: after the first commits, PostgreSQL re-checks the waiting query against the latest row versions, the second caller gets back only one row, and its application check refuses to proceed.

sections.content: **Other index types beyond B-trees**: PostgreSQL supports several specialized index types. **Hash indexes** support only equality lookups (no ranges, no ordering). Before PostgreSQL 10 they were not WAL-logged, so they had to be rebuilt after a crash and did not work on replicas; since PostgreSQL 10 they are crash-safe, but a B-tree is usually just as fast for equality anyway. **GIN (Generalized Inverted Index)** is used for full-text search and JSONB column querying — it maps each word or key to a list of rows containing it. **GiST (Generalized Search Tree)** supports geometric data, nearest-neighbor queries, and IP address range containment. **BRIN (Block Range Index)** is extremely compact and useful for very large tables with naturally ordered data (like time-series), where it stores only the min/max value per block of pages instead of an entry per row. Choosing the right index type is as important as choosing which columns to index.

**Common mistakes and interview traps**: (1) Indexing a low-cardinality column like `status` where 90% of rows are 'active' — the planner ignores it for the common value, because random heap fetches for 90% of rows are slower than a scan. A *partial* index on the rare value (`WHERE status = 'pending'`) is the fix. (2) Forgetting that indexes must be updated on every write — a table with 15 indexes can be several times slower to insert into than one with 2. (3) Using `SELECT *` when the index covers only a subset of columns — forces heap fetches that an index-only scan would avoid. (4) Running huge transactions: they hold locks, block VACUUM, and in undo-log engines (InnoDB, Oracle) the rollback can take as long as the work itself. (5) Setting `fsync = off` to speed up tests and carrying it to production — it risks corruption, not just lost commits; `synchronous_commit = off` is the safe speed knob. (6) Assuming PostgreSQL `REPEATABLE READ` is serializable — it is snapshot isolation: phantom-free (stronger than the standard) but it still allows write skew. And remember the defaults differ: PostgreSQL uses READ COMMITTED, MySQL InnoDB uses REPEATABLE READ.

items: **Atomicity** guarantees all-or-nothing execution. InnoDB/Oracle implement it with undo logs (rollback cost grows with the work done); PostgreSQL writes new row versions and just marks an aborted transaction, so ROLLBACK is near-instant.

**Isolation** levels trade anomalies for throughput. Defaults: Read Committed in PostgreSQL/Oracle/SQL Server, Repeatable Read in MySQL InnoDB. PostgreSQL Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation — no phantoms, but write skew is still possible; only Serializable prevents it.
**Serializable** in PostgreSQL (SSI) aborts conflicting transactions with SQLSTATE 40001 — the application must retry the whole transaction.

**Durability** comes from the WAL: the commit record is fsynced (often via group commit) before COMMIT returns, and recovery replays the log from the last checkpoint. Never set `fsync = off` in production; `synchronous_commit = off` is the safe trade-off.
**MVCC** lets readers and writers proceed without blocking each other by keeping multiple row versions — at the price of dead tuples that VACUUM must reclaim.
**B+ trees** keep all leaves at the same depth, route through internal nodes and link leaves for range scans; with hundreds of keys per page, a billion rows need only 4–5 levels.
**Composite index column order**: equality columns first, the range/ORDER BY column last; an index on `(a, b)` cannot do a normal lookup for `WHERE b = ?` alone.
**Covering and partial indexes** (`INCLUDE`, `WHERE status = 'pending'`) enable index-only scans and keep indexes small; every extra index slows every write.
**DDL is transactional in PostgreSQL** (roll back a failed migration); MySQL and Oracle implicitly commit around DDL.

quiz.question: Which ACID property guarantees that if the server crashes immediately after COMMIT returns, the committed data is still saved?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
quiz.explanation: Durability ensures committed data survives crashes. It is implemented via the write-ahead log (WAL), which is fsynced to disk before COMMIT returns to the application. On recovery, the database replays the WAL to restore the committed state.

quiz.question: Transaction A reads a row. Transaction B updates and commits that row. Transaction A reads the same row again and sees a different value. Which isolation anomaly is this?
options: Dirty read
Non-repeatable read
Phantom read
Serialization failure
quiz.explanation: A non-repeatable read occurs when the same row is read twice within a transaction and yields different values because another transaction committed a change between the two reads. Repeatable Read isolation level prevents this.

quiz.question: Why do B-trees (used in database indexes) have a much larger branching factor than binary trees, typically storing hundreds of keys per node?
options: To reduce memory usage in the buffer pool
To allow faster key comparison using SIMD instructions
To minimize the number of disk page reads per lookup
To support concurrent writers without locking
quiz.explanation: Each B-tree node corresponds to one disk page. A large branching factor means fewer levels in the tree, so a lookup touches fewer disk pages. Disk I/O is orders of magnitude slower than memory access, so minimizing page reads is the primary design goal of B-trees.

quiz.question: You have a composite index on (status, created_at). Which query can use this index efficiently?
options: WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01'
WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at > '2024-01-01'
WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01' AND status = 'pending'
Both B and C
quiz.explanation: The query optimizer can reorder WHERE predicates, so both B and C effectively use the index the same way: the equality predicate on status narrows to a B-tree subtree, then the range predicate on created_at is scanned within that subtree. Option A cannot use a direct descent because the leading column (status) is unconstrained — at best the planner scans the whole index, or (PostgreSQL 18+) skip-scans it once per distinct status value, which is never as efficient as B or C.

quiz.question: Under PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ, two transactions each run "SELECT count(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call" (both see 2), then each sets a *different* doctor off call and commits. What happens?
options: Both commit and zero doctors are left on call — write skew, which snapshot isolation does not prevent
The second UPDATE blocks until the first commits, then fails with a serialization error
The second transaction sees the first one's change because Repeatable Read re-reads modified rows
Both commit safely, because Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL also prevents phantoms
quiz.explanation: The transactions update different rows, so there is no write-write conflict for snapshot isolation to detect, and each one decided based on its own snapshot. Both commit and the invariant breaks — write skew. Only SERIALIZABLE (SSI) detects the read/write dependency cycle and aborts one, or you must lock the rows the decision depends on (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE).

quiz.question: What does MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) primarily eliminate?
options: The need for a write-ahead log
Read-write blocking between concurrent transactions
The need for table-level locks during DDL
Phantom reads at the Read Committed isolation level
quiz.explanation: MVCC allows readers to see a consistent snapshot of data without acquiring locks, while writers create new row versions rather than overwriting. This means readers never block writers and writers never block readers, dramatically increasing concurrency.

quiz.question: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 'Seq Scan' on a 2-million-row table with filter WHERE email = ?. The most effective immediate fix is:
options: Run VACUUM on the table
Increase the work_mem configuration setting
CREATE INDEX on the email column
Rewrite the query as a subquery
quiz.explanation: A sequential scan on a large table for a point lookup on a high-cardinality column means no usable index exists. Creating a B-tree index on email converts the O(n) table scan into an O(log n) index lookup, typically reducing query time by orders of magnitude.

quiz.question: What is a 'phantom read' and which isolation level is guaranteed to prevent it?
options: New rows appearing in a repeated range query due to another transaction's commit; prevented by Serializable
Reading a deleted row; prevented by Repeatable Read
Reading uncommitted data from another transaction; prevented by Read Committed
Two transactions writing the same row concurrently; prevented by Repeatable Read
quiz.explanation: A phantom read occurs when a range query run twice in the same transaction returns different rows because another transaction inserted (or deleted) rows matching the range between the two reads. Only Serializable is required by the SQL standard to prevent phantoms. (PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read happens to prevent them too, but that is stronger than the standard demands.)

quiz.question: Why should you almost never create more than a handful of indexes on a write-heavy table?
options: The query planner cannot consider more than 8 indexes per query
Each index must be updated on every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE, multiplying write I/O
Indexes consume too much memory in the shared buffer pool
More than 5 indexes causes the autovacuum daemon to skip the table
quiz.explanation: Every index is a separate B-tree that must stay synchronized with the heap table. Each INSERT adds a key to every index; each UPDATE that changes an indexed column deletes the old key and inserts a new one in every affected index. On write-heavy tables, this overhead can make writes dramatically slower and even cause the table's write throughput to be index-bound.

quiz.question: An Index Only Scan is faster than an Index Scan because:
options: It uses a hash table instead of a B-tree for lookups
It uses BRIN compression to reduce I/O
It runs in parallel across all CPU cores automatically
It skips the heap entirely — all needed columns are in the index
quiz.explanation: In an Index Only Scan, all columns required by the query (in SELECT, WHERE, and ORDER BY) are present in the index itself. The database finds the rows in the index and returns results without fetching the corresponding heap pages, eliminating the typically expensive random-I/O heap access that makes a plain Index Scan slower.
